s.t: How a log becomes a result

k: mate is a self-hosted platform for process mining: it turns event logs into process models, performance figures, conformance results, and drift reports, and it treats every analysis as an installable module. | role | what mate gives you | | --- | --- | | analyst | a guided path from an uploaded log to charts, models, and dashboards — no code. | | researcher | a runtime for your method: scheduling, progress, caching, isolation, a settings ui, dashboard cards, and citations that travel with the code. | | operator | one compose stack to deploy, back up, and monitor. | file · xes, csv, xml, or ocel 2.0 import job · parse, normalise, write parquet parquet log · the event table plus cached case aggregates module runs · one per (log, module), started when a module is first opened filters & edits · committing a filter re-runs the modules you have already opened module results · cached per (log, module) panels, widgets, and datasets mate ai · aggregates only, behind the data wall dashboards · cards from any module, on one canvas three properties shape everything else in this manual: local-first. logs, results, and metadata stay on your host. nothing is sent anywhere unless you configure an external service on purpose. modular. the bundled analyses use the same sdk, loader, and gating rules as modules you install later. there are no privileged hooks. typed end to end. pydantic defines the api, one openapi schema generates the web app's types, and module authors program against protocols. | goal | read | | --- | --- | | run mate | install and start | | see it work once | your first analysis | | import and explore real logs | using mate | | build a module | your first module | | call mate from a script or an agent | rest api · mcp server | | run a deployment | deployment · troubleshooting | | work on the platform itself | how mate works · contributing | process mining has its own vocabulary; mate adds a few terms. | term | meaning | | --- | --- | | event log | a table of events: what happened, when, and in which case. | | case | a process instance (an order, a claim) identified by a case id; its events form a trace. | | activity | the label of what happened — registered, approved. | | variant | the sequence of activities a case followed. cases that took the same path share one. | | directly-follows graph (dfg) | activities as nodes, observed successions as edges. | | petri net · process tree · bpmn | model notations. discovery produces them; conformance replays a log against one. | | conformance | fitness (was every trace replayable), precision, and the deviations found. | | concept drift | a change in the process over time: a new branch, a vanishing activity, shifted timing. | | ocel | object-centric event log: events relate to many objects of different types, so there is no single case notion. | | module | the unit of extension: a folder with a manifest, a handler class, and optionally a frontend. | | manifest | manifest.yaml — identity, log requirements, dependencies, capabilities, frontend, citations. | | precompute | the job a module runs for a log to fill its cache. it starts the first time the module is opened (or right after import, for the few *eager* modules), so every later open is instant. | | capability | a named request/response function one module publishes for another. | | event bus | in-process pub/sub; modules emit and subscribe to declared topics. | | job | a persisted, observable long operation: import, precompute, install, re-import. | | dataset | a typed data output (table, graph, kpi, tree, blob) the platform renders itself. | | widget | a dashboard card a module ships as a react component. | | guidance | cached, module-scoped ai explanation, generated on demand. | | data wall | the rule that raw event rows never reach an ai model — mate ai or mcp. |

from a clean host to a logged-in workspace. the whole stack is one compose file. docker desktop or docker engine with compose v2. free ports 3000 (web), 8000 (api), 8080 (keycloak). ~3 gb for images, plus room for your data. python, node, uv, and pnpm are only needed for host development (contributing). clone and enter the repository. git clone https://github.com/process-science-community/mate.git mate
cd mate create the environment file, then rotate its two secrets before the stack is reachable by anyone else. cp .env.example .env build and start everything. make up open http://localhost:3000 and sign in as admin@flows-funds.local with flowsfunds. keycloak forces a password change on first login. add users in the keycloak console at http://localhost:8080/admin (admin / admin), realm flows-funds. the seeded account is not an administrator. the admin realm role gates the admin pages and the metadata export; assign it in the keycloak console, then sign in again. | stage | what happens | time | | --- | --- | --- | | images build | api, web, keycloak | 3–8 min | | databases start | app-db, keycloak-db | seconds | | realm import | keycloak imports the realm on an empty database | ~30 s | | api boots | migrations run, then the loader builds one virtual environment per bundled module | up to 10 min | | web boots | next.js starts and bundles module frontends | ~1 min | the api health check deliberately allows ten minutes for this. later boots hash each module's dependency block, skip what is unchanged, and start in seconds. | command | what you get | | --- | --- | | make up | base compose file: production-style images, detached. the default. | | make up-dev | base plus compose.dev.yml: hot reload inside docker. | | make dev | host dev servers (api + web) with the fastest reload. needs uv, pnpm, python 3.12. | | prod overlay | docker-compose.prod.yml: caddy with tls, one public origin, no public app ports. see deployment. | terminal make down                     # stop (keeps volumes and data)
make up                       # start again, reusing module environments
docker compose logs -f api    # follow the api log (also: web, keycloak) make clean wipes event logs, module results, the metadata database, and the keycloak volume. this cannot be undone. for a workshop without keycloak, demo_mode=true signs everyone in as a fixed local user. never enable it on a shared deployment — the mcp server refuses the demo token by design.

one log from import to dashboard: import it, monitor the jobs, open a module, and build a board. open processes and click import event log. drop a file: .xes, .xes.gz, .csv, .xml, .json, .jsonocel, .xmlocel, .sqlite, and .gz/.bz2/.xz/.zip variants. the upload stages, then the server probes a few hundred events and proposes column roles. confirm the mapping — the only step where a wrong answer costs a re-import. submit. the wizard switches to a live checklist: reading, processing, saving. the process is ready the moment it is saved. | role | required | unlocks | | --- | --- | --- | | case_id | yes | cases, variants, everything case-scoped. | | activity | yes | activities, dfgs, models, complexity. | | timestamp | yes | ordering, time bounds, trends. | | end_timestamp | no | durations, waiting times, most performance metrics. | | resource | no | actor analyses; actor_performance requires it. | each row shows how the proposal was made — user → *your choice*, exact → *matched*, fuzzy → *guessed*, fallback → *inferred from data* — and low-confidence guesses are flagged. when a provider is configured, the wizard re-proposes those rows automatically and marks them ai. xes and ocel files carry their own schema and skip this step. the checklist ends when the file is saved, and the process is ready from that moment — nothing waits on modules. they compute lazily: each runs the first time you open it. the few marked *eager* (discovery) also warm up in the background right after the import, and show in the jobs drawer; a module that fails never affects the log. | status | meaning | | --- | --- | | importing | the file is parsed and normalised. | | ready | saved and open. each module computes the first time you open it. | | failed | the import failed; the row shows why, with a retry. | click the row. the process page opens on the module grid, grouped by category. | card state | meaning | | --- | --- | | available | everything the module needs is present — shown without a badge. | | limited | an optional module dependency is missing; the module runs with less context. | | unavailable | the log model, a required column, a minimum count, or a hard dependency does not match; the tooltip names the reason. | | disabled | turned off for your account. | | computing | its job is running right now. the card stays openable and shows the progress. | | failed | its last run failed. open it to see why and retry. | open discovery for the process as a directly-follows graph (and petri net, process tree, heuristics net, or bpmn), performance for throughput and bottlenecks, complexity v2 for a metric suite. the first time you open a module for a log it computes: you see live progress with a cancel, and the page appears when it finishes. later opens are instant, and the result refreshes by itself after the log's data changes. each page is the module's own panel inside the platform's frame: breadcrumb, version, configure (a form generated from the module's schema, saved per user), an info hint with the module's description and citations, and a how to use button that opens the module's guide beside the page: what the module needs, every setting, and how to read each view. open dashboards and create a board, or start from a template. in edit mode, drag cards from the palette: widgets modules ship, and datasets the platform renders. select a card to set its options; the board's filter bar scopes every card at once. share the board read-only with a user or a team. the mate ai panel attaches context from the current view — process, open module, page — and answers with links that navigate the app. if no provider is configured it says so and links to *settings → ai*. the assistant reads aggregates and cached module outputs only. raw event rows never enter a prompt, which is what lets it sit next to confidential data. | action | what the platform did | | --- | --- | | dropped a file | staged, probed, parsed, normalised, written as parquet under data/users/{uid}/event_logs/{log_id}/. | | confirmed a mapping | column roles stored on the log; a log.imported event dispatched. | | watched a checklist | the file was saved and the process became ready; only eager modules (discovery) started in the background. | | opened a module | the first time, the platform ran its job (and any module it depends on) with live progress, then mounted its panel on the cached result. | | filtered the log | the filter was committed and the modules you had already opened re-ran, so results match what you see; the rest compute when opened. |

the wizard accepts five format families, probes them server-side, and writes nothing until you confirm the interpretation. | format | extensions | mapping step | | --- | --- | --- | | xes | .xes, .xes.gz | none — the file carries its own schema | | csv | .csv | required: case id, activity, timestamp | | xml | .xml | required: the event element, then column roles | | json event log | .json | required: the event path, then column roles | | ocel 2.0 | .jsonocel, .xmlocel, .sqlite | none — object-centric structure is in the file | all formats accept .gz, .bz2, .xz, and .zip wrappers. an archive holding several logs (.zip, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz – a bpi challenge download, say) opens a picker first. every log in it starts selected; readmes, licences and nested archives are listed with the reason they are skipped. each log you keep is unpacked on its own, gets its own mapping step, and becomes a separate process. unpacking is bounded by the zip-bomb guards in configuration. choose a file — drop it on the zone or pick it from disk. upload — streams to a staging area with byte-level progress; nothing is parsed yet. probe — the server samples a few hundred events and proposes column roles. map — confirm the roles and the format-specific extras. import — parse, normalise, write parquet. the process is ready as soon as it is saved; modules compute when first opened. staged files live under data/staging/{user}/{token}/ and are removed after two hours, so an abandoned wizard leaves nothing behind. | role | required | unlocks | | --- | --- | --- | | case_id | yes | cases, variants, everything case-scoped. | | activity | yes | activities, dfgs, models, complexity. | | timestamp | yes | ordering, time bounds, trends. | | end_timestamp | no | durations, waiting times, performance metrics. | | resource | no | actor analyses (actor_performance requires it). | | cost | no | cost aggregations where a module uses them. | format extras appear where they apply: csv delimiter, xml event element, a json array key, and an optional timestamp format (offered for every mapping-based format, used when the sample is ambiguous). each row carries a confidence chip — user → *your choice*, exact → *matched*, fuzzy → *guessed*, fallback → *inferred from data*. when a provider is configured the wizard re-proposes low-confidence rows automatically and marks them ai. any edit re-opens the confirmation gate; confirm mapping unlocks the import, and start import runs it. a wrong timestamp format is the most common import mistake. if the probe preview shows dates but a module later reports empty time bounds, remap the roles in the log's settings tab. the checklist mirrors the real job: *uploading file*, *reading columns*, *reading data*, *processing events*, *saving*. when *saving* is done the process is open; there is no module step to wait for, because modules compute the first time you open them. the few *eager* ones (discovery) warm up in the background and appear in the jobs drawer. fixable problems are repaired rather than rejected — case-insensitive duplicate columns are merged, values are coerced to their column type, timestamps normalised — and the count of fixes is reported. a module that fails is marked and never affects the log. | action | where | effect | | --- | --- | --- | | re-run import | row menu, or *maintenance* in the log's settings | rebuilds from the retained original upload. | | remap columns | log settings → *column roles* | forces new roles and re-runs the import. | | duplicate | row menu | clones the log row and directory — useful for comparing filtered views. | | rename | row menu → *rename* (dialog) | display name only; urls keep the log id. | | delete | row menu | cancels its jobs, removes the data on disk and the s3 prefix. |

the card is marked limited and the module runs with less context. | folders nest freely; moving one refuses to move it into its own descendant. deleting a folder cascades to its subfolders and logs, after a confirmation that names the count. the tree supports drag-and-drop reordering and a *move to* row action. the list reads ?q= and ?status= from the url, so a filtered view is a shareable link. a watched folder turns a directory — or an s3 prefix — into an import source. | aspect | behaviour | | --- | --- | | trigger | a poller compares the source against its ledger every 30 s (60 s in continuous mode). | | modes | manual (scan on demand), interval (every n seconds), continuous. | | deduplication | watched_folder_files records size plus mtime (local) or etag (s3), so each file imports once. | | source files | never moved, renamed, or deleted. | | mapping | a per-format default mapping is required — there is no wizard for an unattended file. | the card per folder shows mode, interval, last scan, and a status badge (active, paused, error), with scan, pause/resume, and delete actions. for a local path, the directory must exist inside the api container — bind-mount it. | section | holds | | --- | --- | | general | display name and description. | | column roles | required and optional roles with confidence hints; remap re-runs the import. | | data quality | completeness per column. | | source & schema | original filename, format, import time, time bounds, per-column labels. | | edit history | every cell edit with its timestamp. | | maintenance | re-run import, delete. |

the process page is the workspace for one log. its tabs are url-backed, so any view — a filtered event list, a variant, an activity — is a shareable link. the breadcrumb carries the name and the overview tab opens with the stat strip (format, cases, events, variants, date range, import time); ocel logs are also badged object-centric. the data tabs — events, variants, activities (or objects/events/relationships on an ocel log) — stay disabled until the log is ready; overview and settings are always available. banners appear for a mapping that needs review, an import in progress, and a failure. | tab | contents | | --- | --- | | overview | stat strip, then the module grid with search; disabled cards state their reason. | | events | virtualised event table with search, per-column filters, sorting, and edit mode. | | variants | aggregated variants: cases, average duration, share of cases, last seen. | | activities | activity list with event counts and editable display names. | | settings | everything in log settings. | ocel logs swap the middle tabs for objects, events, and relationships, driven by the log's own parquet schema. | control | behaviour | | --- | --- | | cross-column search | debounced 300 ms. | | missing-values switch | shows only rows with empty cells. | | column filters | operators per column type — string: contains, equals, is_null, is_not_null; numeric, duration, and datetime: equals, gte, lte, is_null, is_not_null; enum and boolean: equals, is_null, is_not_null. | | apply / restore | commits the filter to the log (re-running modules), or restores the unfiltered view. | | case chip | arriving with ?case_id= restricts the table to that case. | | paging | 25, 50, 100, or 200 rows. | the variants tab filters by activity and minimum case count, sorts by cases, duration, or recency, and shows each variant's share of all cases. opening a variant gives its sequence, a duration histogram, attribute breakdowns, and the list of its cases. the activities tab lists each activity with its event count and lets you set a display name used across the app. wherever a module renders an activity or a variant, the label links into the matching view, carrying the standard drill parameters (activity, case, variant, object_type, ts_from/ts_to, view, metric; from/to name the two ends of a graph edge). that is what makes a chart a starting point rather than an endpoint.

the assistant runs in a right-hand panel: context-aware, restricted by a data wall, and configured per account. | element | behaviour | | --- | --- | | context | attached automatically from the url: current page, log, and the module open on the page. | | starters | suggested questions that change with context; the strip hides itself once you have asked there. | | answers | streamed over server-sent events, with navigation chips that deep-link into the app. | | guidance cards | per-module and per-process explanations you can generate, refresh, or regenerate; cached with the module's results. | | no provider | the panel says so and links to *settings → ai*; the starter chips are disabled. | | provider | notes | | --- | --- | | anthropic | native transport; no embeddings. | | openai | also used for embeddings. | | unigpt | institutional gateway; base url required. | | custom | any openai-compatible endpoint. | the form takes a key (masked afterwards; leaving it blank keeps the stored key), a base url where needed, then *fetch models* to populate the pickers. when an administrator controls the ai configuration, the panel is read-only and says so. modules can go further: ai_models in their manifest renders their own provider and model selectors, and self_hosted: true gives a module an isolated key field. neither mate ai nor the mcp server can read raw event rows. the restriction is structural: the context built for an ai request has its event-log accessors replaced by objects that raise on any access. what reaches a model is aggregates, cached module outputs, and metadata the page already shows. one switch decides how much context is used, off by default: *access process data* enables both the process list (which logs exist and their headline figures) and activity and variant aggregates, capped at 40 activities and the top 15 variants and skipped for ocel logs.

actor performance explains why work waits between two steps of a case. for every step and its next step it classifies how the work moved between people: the same actor carried on, the same actor did something else in between, or another actor took over, who was idle, busy or doing other work first. it then shows how much waiting time each kind of behaviour contributes. a transition is slow and the averages do not say why. here you see whether the wait comes from handovers that sit idle in a queue, from actors who interrupt their own work, or from actors who did other work first. you want to separate a handover problem from a capacity problem before you change staffing or rules. you want the waiting times of the steps of a process, the cycle time of cases or the bottlenecks without the actor view: use performance. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity, timestamp and resource columns, at least 100 events and at least 5 cases. a lifecycle column is used when the log has one. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. the analysis runs in a neo4j graph engine. it is a separate server that is not part of mate, and all users share it. an administrator switches it on with the graph profile of the docker stack, or on a development machine with the docker run command that the panel shows. while the engine cannot be reached, the panel shows "graph sidecar not running" with these instructions, checks again every few seconds, and keeps the run button off. a wrong password shows "neo4j rejected the credentials". nothing is precomputed. a run starts only when you press run analysis, as a background job with progress messages, and the panel shows the result of your last run and when it ran. only one analysis runs at a time, across all users, so yours can wait in line. events without a resource are left out, because the analysis needs to know who did each step. the panel says how many were excluded. a filter bar above the panel (add filter and a time range you confirm with apply) narrows the events of the next run. results are kept for each filter on its own and show only while the same filter is on. the filter is temporary: reloading the page clears it. everything stays on your servers: the graph engine belongs to mate, the graph is cleared before and after every run, and the results are kept only for your account. if an administrator points the module at a remote neo4j server, the data goes there. two fields sit under the title. pressing the run button saves their values, so the next run starts with them. after a run, a badge "re-run to apply" appears while the fields differ from the result on screen. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | min. transition frequency | 0 | only transitions that occur at least this often are analysed. 0 keeps every transition. on a log with many rare transitions, a higher value shortens the run. | | max. transitions | 150 | the most transitions that are analysed (10 to 1000), the most frequent first. when the run reaches the cap, the tile transitions shows a "capped" badge. | the button reads run analysis first, re-run once a result exists and "running…" during a run. while it runs, the panel shows the current stage, a percentage and a bar. the stages read-only. the first two fields below repeat the panel's fields and start from the same values. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | minimum transition frequency | 0 | the same as min. transition frequency in the panel, from 0 to 100000. the paper used 1000 on the full bpic17 log. | | max transitions to extract | 150 | the same as max. transitions in the panel. | | the classes in a card "what the classes mean". after a run it shows six tiles, the behaviour mix and the transitions. each transition, a step followed by the next step of the same case, falls into exactly one class. continuation: the same actor continued directly with the next step, with nothing else in between in their own work. interruption: the same actor did both steps but worked on something else in between. handover (idle): another actor took over, and they had finished their previous task before the work became available, or it is the first work of that actor in the log. handover (prioritized): another actor took over, and they were in the middle of another task when the work became available. they did this step as the next piece of their work. handover (deprioritized): another actor took over, but only after they had started other work that began after the work became available. unclassified: a transition that no class matched. it should be rare. the wait of a transition is the time between the timestamps of the two events. events, cases and actors count what the run used, after the events without a resource were left out. task instances counts the stretches of work in the graph, where a stretch is a run of events that one actor performs on one case without doing anything else in between. transitions counts the transitions that were analysed, and a "capped" badge means the run reached max. transitions. runtime is the duration of the run. a line above the mix says how many events were excluded for lack of a resource. a bar shows the share of each class among all analysed transitions. under it, one card per class that occurs gives the number of transitions, their share in percent, a bar for the mean wait and the mean wait as a duration. hover a card to read the class description. the mix covers the analysed transitions only, so a minimum frequency or the cap leaves the rare transitions out of it. one row per analysed transition, written as the first activity, an arrow and the next activity. when the log has a lifecycle column, each activity carries its transition after a dot, such as ·complete. a row shows its count, its mean wait and a small bar with the behaviour mix. click a row to open one card per class with its count and share, and the mean, the median and the 90th percentile of the wait. the box "filter activities…" narrows the list to transitions whose activities contain your text. the menu sorts by "most frequent", the default, or "slowest (mean)". at most 150 rows show at a time, and a note says how many more there are. read the share and the mean wait of a class together. a rare class with a huge wait means something other than a common class that is only a little slow. the wait is the difference between two timestamps. in a log with only completion times it includes the time the next step took. with start and complete events, look at the rows that go from a complete event to a start event for the pure waiting. continuation and interruption involve one actor only, so their waits are not handover queues: the actor did the next step themselves, directly or after other work. use min. transition frequency and max. transitions to keep a run short on a log with many different transitions. large logs also need much memory for the graph engine: about 2 gb of heap for small and medium logs, and about 10 gb for a log of over a million events. an administrator sets it. each run replaces the stored result for its filter. to compare two settings, note the numbers before you run again. a run that fails says why, for example that the graph engine cannot be reached, that the import folder cannot be written, or that no events were left after leaving out those without a resource. the module follows klijn, tentina, fahland and mannhardt (2024), who decompose waiting times by actor behaviour. a run writes the log, with the events that have a resource, to a file for the graph engine, builds an event knowledge graph of the cases and the actors in neo4j with the promg library, and groups the events into task instances. a task instance is a run of events that one actor performs on one case and that follow each other in the actor's own work. it then labels every directly-follows step of a case with one class, by comparing the events and the task instances of the two actors. the labels are applied in this order, and a later label replaces an earlier one: continuation, interruption, handover idle, handover prioritized and handover deprioritized. finally it reads the wait of every step, the difference of the two timestamps, and gives the count, the share, the mean, the median and the 90th percentile for each transition and class. the log-wide mix weights each transition by its number of steps. the graph is cleared before and after every run, so it holds no data between runs. the formal citation is in the info popover next to the module name.

agentsimulator learns from your log how the people and systems in your process work: who does which activity, when they work, how long it takes and who hands work to whom. it then generates synthetic logs of the process and scores how closely they match a held-out part of your real log. use it to see how well the behaviour of the process can be reproduced, and to get simulated logs. you want to know whether a model of agents with working calendars and handovers can reproduce your process, and in which respect it falls short: the order of activities, the timing or the congestion. you want to compare the two ways of handing over work, autonomous or centrally orchestrated, by how well each reproduces the real log. you want synthetic logs that follow the behaviour of the real process, for tools outside mate. you want to understand the real waiting times or who hands over to whom: use performance, or actor performance for the actor view. agentsimulator reproduces the process as it was learned and has no setting that changes staffing, calendars or rules. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity, timestamp and resource columns, at least 200 events and at least 20 cases. an end_timestamp column is used when the log has one. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. most logs have one timestamp per event. then mate takes the gap to the next event of the case as the duration of an activity, so the working time and the waiting time cannot be told apart, while the duration of whole cases stays exact. with real end timestamps the durations are used as they are. events without a resource count as one agent called undefined. events without a case, an activity or a start time are left out. nothing is precomputed. a run starts when you press run simulation, here or on a dashboard card, as a background job with progress messages. it can take several minutes, and the panel shows the result of the last run. this page has no filter bar, and the filters of a dashboard do not apply to it. a filter applied on the log's events tab narrows the events that the simulation reads. everything runs on your mate server, and nothing is sent to an outside service. four options sit under the title. pressing the run button saves them, and a dashboard run uses the saved values. after a run, a badge "settings changed" appears while the options differ from the result on screen. the same four fields are on the module page. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | simulated logs | 5 | how many synthetic logs are generated (1 to 10). they are repetitions of the same model, and the simulation is random, so more runs give a steadier fidelity score and take longer. | | determine configuration automatically | off | the module simulates a validation slice of its learning data, the last fifth of the cases by case id, with all four combinations of handover type and extraneous delays and keeps the one whose case durations are closest to the real ones. this is the most accurate and much slower. while it is on, the next two switches are greyed out and ignored. | | central orchestration | off | off means autonomous: every agent decides on its own to whom it hands the work over, following the handovers seen in the log. on means orchestrated: a central orchestrator assigns each next activity to a suitable agent. | | discover extraneous delays | off | also models waiting time that the availability of the resources does not explain. this is slower. | the button reads run simulation first, re-run once a result exists and "running…" during a run, with the current stage and a bar. cancel a run in the jobs drawer of the sidebar. open module settings in the sidebar and choose this module. the configuration card has the four fields above, and save configuration saves them. an administrator can lock the card, which makes it read-only. before the first run, the page reads "no simulation yet" with a run simulation button. after a run, it shows three cards. the badges name the mode, autonomous, orchestrated or main_results for the automatic choice, the number of logs and the duration of the run. five tiles score the simulated logs against the test log. each is a distance, so lower is better, and each shows the mean over the simulated logs, the standard deviation and an info icon. ngd, the n-gram distribution: how different the frequencies of every three consecutive activities are, from 0 for the same order of work to 1. aedd, the absolute event distribution: how different the times of the events on the calendar are, in hours. cedd, the circadian event distribution: how different the times of day of the events are, in hours. it checks the working hours. redd, the relative event distribution: how different the times of the events measured from the start of their case are, in hours. ctdd, the cycle time distribution: how different the durations of whole cases are, in hours. it reflects the processing times together with the congestion. ngd is a total-variation distance, and the other four are earth mover's distances. below the tiles, four figures give the number of test cases and their events, the average number of cases per simulated log (sim cases / run) and the median cycle time of the real and of the simulated logs in hours. the real log in all comparisons is the test log, roughly the newest fifth of the events of your log. the model learns from the earlier part, see method. five tabs compare the test log with the average of the simulated logs. cycle time: how many cases fall into each of 20 duration classes, the last of which takes all the longest cases. a caption gives the median and the 90th percentile of both. arrivals: new cases started per day, or per week when the span exceeds 90 days. each log counts from its own first case, so a different start date does not matter. activity mix: how often each of the 12 most frequent activities of the test log occurs, per log. time of day: events by hour of the day, in utc. it shows whether the simulation respects working hours. handovers: two tables of the probability that work passes from one resource to another, for the real log and for the simulation. they cover the eight busiest resources of the test log, and a darker cell is a higher probability. each cell shows a percentage, hovering gives the exact value, and long names are cut. the rows are scaled to sum to 1 among these eight. one button per run, such as "run 1 · 120 cases", opens a dialog where you choose csv or xes for that run. a download holds at most the first 20,000 events of the run. the csv has the columns case_id, activity, resource, start and end, and the xes file carries the end time as the event time and the start time as an extra attribute. below the buttons, a table previews the first 50 events of run 1. each card has an info icon with a short explanation and an arrow (open in module) that opens this page. the cards ignore the filters of their dashboard, because the result belongs to the whole log. simulation fidelity: the five tiles of the panel. cycle time – real vs simulated: the duration classes of the cycle time tab. case arrivals – real vs simulated: the arrivals chart, with its days or weeks numbered from the start. a card without a result reads "no simulation yet for this log". its run simulation button starts a run with the saved options, and configure opens this page. while a run is going, whoever started it, such a card shows the progress, and it also says when the last run failed or was cancelled. use the scores to compare configurations on one log. the time measures are in hours, so their size depends on how long cases and periods are in your process, and values from different logs do not compare. raise simulated logs for a steadier score, and expect a longer run. the automatic choice is the slowest, so try autonomous and orchestrated first if time is short. the test log is roughly the newest fifth of the events. if the process changed in that period, the model learned the old behaviour, and the distances grow. with a single timestamp per event, the simulated cases have realistic lengths, but the split of working and waiting time is not reliable. the simulated logs contain no real cases, but they carry the real activity names and the behaviour learned from the log. check them before you share them. a run that fails reports the reason, and the end of the simulator's output is part of the message when it produced no logs. mate computes the five distances itself with numpy and scipy, in the way the paper defines them. the values can differ slightly from the paper's reference code. the module follows kirchdorfer, blümel, kampik, van der aa and stuckenschmidt (2024). it first brings the log into one table of case, activity, resource, start and end. the events are ordered by their end time, the first 80% are the learning data and the last 20% are the test log. a case that straddles the cut is left out of both parts. the last fifth of the learning cases, in the order of their case ids, is kept as a validation log. from the learning data it discovers one agent per resource, with roles and working calendars, the distribution of the duration of each activity per agent, the probabilities of the next activity and of the handover between agents, the activities that must come first, the largest number of repetitions of an activity in a case and the arrival process of cases. it then simulates the process with these agents over the period of the test log. a simulated log has as many cases as the test log, and the simulation is repeated for the chosen number of logs. with the automatic choice, the module simulates the validation log in all four combinations and keeps the one with the smallest cycle-time distance. the five scores compare each simulated log with the test log, and the panel shows their mean and standard deviation. the formal citation is in the info popover next to the module name.

complexity puts numbers on how tangled your process is. it scores the log with entropy, size, variation and pentland measures and lists them in two tables, so you can compare processes or process versions and see how much variability a log carries. you want to compare processes or versions of a process objectively, for example before and after a standardisation effort, by scoring each log with the same measures. you want to know early whether a log will produce an unreadable spaghetti model, before you discover one. you want to see how the complexity develops over time. use complexity over time. for a larger suite of 28 measures including trace distances, use complexity v2. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 50 events and at least 2 cases. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. the first time you open the module for a process, mate computes the measures. it shows "computing complexity…" with a progress bar and a cancel button before the panel appears, and afterwards the page opens at once. a filter bar above the panel (add filter and a time range you confirm with apply) narrows the log, and the module recomputes on the filtered events. it is temporary: reloading the page clears it. a second view, enriched epa, exists only for logs that carry a complete set of xes attributes (see reading the results). without them the panel shows the basic view only. the panel has no controls apart from the two tabs described below. the module has one setting, on its module page: open module settings in the sidebar and choose this module. an administrator can lock the configuration card, which makes it read-only. save with save configuration. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | exponential forgetting k | 1.0 | the coefficient k of the exponentially forgetting sequence entropy (0.1 to 10 in steps of 0.1). larger values make older events count less. the original paper uses 1. the panel shows the value in the row's name. saving does not recompute results that already exist; the new value applies the next time the measures are computed, for example after the log's data has changed. | a badge above the tables tells which attribute set the module found: "enriched attribute set detected", or "basic only (xes standard attributes missing)". with the enriched set there are two tabs, basic and enriched epa, each with the same two tables; otherwise there is one view. enriched epa needs these xes attributes, on traces variant, concept:name, creator and variant-index, and on events time:timestamp, resource, lifecycle:transition, concept:name, activity and org:resource. it builds the automaton behind the entropies with steps told apart by those attributes. the entropies and pentland's task complexity are recomputed on that automaton, and all other measures are the same in both views. most measures have an info icon with a short explanation and the author who introduced the measure. one row per measure, with its value and its normalised (0–1) form. all four are computed on the log's extended prefix automaton (epa), in which traces that share a beginning share states, so the entropy tells how much the recorded behaviour branches. variant entropy: how much the structure branches, counted in states. it ignores how often each path is taken. sequence entropy: the same entropy weighted by the number of events instead of states, so it also reflects how frequent each prefix is. sequence entropy (linear forgetting) and sequence entropy (exponential forgetting, k=1): sequence entropy in which an event counts less the older it is. the linear weight falls from 1 for the latest event to 0 for the earliest, and the exponential weight is e to the power of minus k times the relative age. they have no info icon. higher entropy means less predictable behaviour. the normalised value divides by the largest possible entropy, so logs of different sizes can be compared on it; the raw value grows with the size of the log. one row per measure with its value and a short description. magnitude: the number of events. support: the number of cases. variety: the number of distinct activities. these are size measures. level of detail: the average number of distinct activities per case. time granularity: the mean over cases of the shortest gap between two consecutive events, shown as a duration. it tells how fine-grained the timestamps are. structure: 1 minus the distinct directly-follows connections divided by the square of the number of activities. near 1 the behaviour is sparse and structured, near 0 almost any activity can follow any other. affinity: the average similarity of the directly-follows patterns of two cases, over all pairs. homogeneous logs score high. trace length: the shortest, the average and the longest case, as min / avg / max. distinct traces: the number of distinct variants, that is of different activity sequences, as a share of the number of cases, in percent. 100% means every case took its own path, and 25% means that each path is taken by four cases on average. deviation from random: 1 minus the distance between the shares of transitions and an even spread over all pairs of activities. close to 1 the transitions are spread almost evenly, like random behaviour; lower, a few transitions dominate. lempel-ziv complexity: the number of phrases needed to describe the stream of all events in time order without repetition. repetitive behaviour needs few, random-looking behaviour many. pentland's task complexity: the sum of the frequencies of the leaf states of the prefix automaton. it has no info icon. pentland's process complexity: 10^(0.08·(1 + e − v)) with e distinct directly-follows connections and v distinct activities, an estimate of the number of routes through the process. a log with very many connections shows "–", because the value would exceed what can be represented. a "–" in any row means the measure is undefined for this log, for example affinity with fewer than two cases. cards follow the filters of their dashboard. each has an info icon with a short explanation and an arrow (open in module) that opens this page. both cards use the basic view. complexity metrics: up to eight tiles: magnitude, variety, distinct traces, avg trace len, variant entropy, sequence entropy, lempel–ziv and pentland, which is the process complexity. the two entropies are the normalised values. until you choose, a card shows all eight. the figures list in the card's settings has one checkbox per tile, where avg trace len reads avg trace length and pentland reads pentland process complexity. it starts with sequence entropy, lempel-ziv and pentland process complexity unticked, and once you change any box the card shows exactly the ticked tiles. each tile has an info icon with the explanation and source of the measure. entropy comparison: a bar chart from 0 to 1 of the normalised variant entropy, sequence entropy and the linear and exponential forgetting variants. the module also offers the dataset complexity metrics in the cards & data palette of a dashboard. the measures disagree by design, because they capture different kinds of complexity. compare two logs on the same measure rather than looking for one overall score, and read a change over versions rather than a single value. when logs differ in size, compare the normalised entropies and the ratio measures, such as distinct traces, structure and affinity, instead of the raw sizes and the raw entropies. the lempel-ziv measure runs over all events in time order as one stream, so cases that overlap in time influence each other. on logs with more than 4,000 distinct directly-follows patterns, affinity uses the most frequent ones and is an approximation. everything is computed from the activity names and the timestamps. the enriched epa view is the only place where other attributes enter. the measures describe the log; they do not say whether a process is good or bad. for the structure of the process use discovery. the module follows augusto, mendling, vidgof and wurm (2022), whose entropy measures are computed on the extended prefix automaton of the log, and the size, variation and distance measures collected from günther (2009), van der aalst (2016), pentland (2003) and hærem et al. (2015). the implementation ports the reference code of rüschel and langer. the formal citation is in the info popover next to the module name. the variant entropy is the graph entropy |s|·log|s| minus the sum of |p|·log|p| over the partitions p of the automaton's states s. the sequence entropy uses the number of events in each partition instead of the number of states, and the forgetting variants weight each event by its recency before summing. normalised entropies divide by the largest possible value. lempel-ziv counts the phrases of the lz76 parse of the time-ordered stream of activities.

complexity over time shows whether your process is getting simpler or more tangled. it cuts the log into time slices, scores each slice with the measures of the complexity module and plots the metrics you choose as a trend, with optional bands for concept drift found by cv4cdd. you want to know whether a redesign, an automation rollout or a standardisation effort actually made the process simpler, for this log. how unpredictable the recorded behaviour is, measured on the log's extended prefix automaton (epa), in which traces that share a beginning share states (augusto et al., 2022). var-e conformance checking replays your event log against a reference bpmn model that you upload. you get the fitness and precision of the model, the share of cases that follow it, and the places where cases deviate, painted onto the diagram. you have a model of how the process should run, such as a designed process, a policy or a standard, and you want to know how closely the recorded cases follow it. you want to find where reality departs from it: the activities and the variants with the most deviations. you have no model yet. open the bpmn view of discovery, save the diagram with download bpmn and upload it here, or draw your own. a mined model mainly reflects the log it came from, so a compliance check is most useful with a model that states what should happen. you want to compare two groups of cases or see how the process runs without a model. use process comparison or discovery. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 50 events and at least 2 cases. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. you need a reference model: a bpmn 2.0 file ending in .bpmn or .xml with at least one labelled task. mate refuses a file it cannot read ("not a readable bpmn model") or one without labelled tasks. the model belongs to this log and your account; it is not shared with other logs. task names in the model must match the activity names in the log. they are compared exactly after trimming spaces, collapsing repeated spaces and ignoring upper and lower case. there is no fuzzy matching, so one wrong letter makes a different activity. nothing is precomputed. a check runs when you start it, as a background job with progress messages, and a freshly uploaded model starts one automatically. this page has no filter bar. a filter applied on the log's events tab narrows the events that are replayed. the reference model card holds the model controls and the technique. upload bpmn adds a model. it becomes the active model and a run starts at once, and a message confirms it with the number of tasks, for example reference model "order.bpmn" ready (14 tasks). a file with the name of an existing model replaces it. file names are reduced to letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores. run conformance appears once a model exists and starts a check with the chosen technique. it reads "running…" while a run is in progress. the list shows every uploaded model with its size and an active badge. choose one to make it active. the trash icon deletes a model from this log after you confirm. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | technique | token-based replay | how cases are replayed: token-based replay or alignments (precise). it is locked while a run is in progress. results are kept per model and technique, so switching to a combination you have not run shows "reference model ready" and a run conformance button. | | heatmap | on | in the diagram's graph settings: colours the tasks by their deviations. | | deviation counts | on | in the diagram's graph settings: puts a count badge on the tasks. | open module settings in the sidebar and choose this module. the values in its configuration card apply to the next run, and saving does not start one. an administrator can lock the card, which makes it read-only. save with save configuration. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | conformance technique | token-based replay | the technique used when a request does not name one: the dashboard cards and the mate ai summary. the panel always starts on token-based replay and sends its own choice. | | conforming-trace threshold | 1.0 | a case counts as conforming when its fitness is at or above this value (0 to 1 in steps of 0.05). it sets the conforming traces tile. | | precision – max events | 150000 | above this many events the token-replay precision is skipped (0 to 5000000). set 0 to always compute it. | | alignments – max cases | 2000 | alignments are refused above this many cases (100 to 100000). | | alignments – max variants | 300 | alignments are refused above this many distinct variants (50 to 20000). | an amber notice reading "activity names don't fully line up" appears when the model and the log disagree about activity names. it lists the model tasks that never occur in the log, which always show as deviations, and the log activities that are not in the model. check it first: a naming problem is the most common reason for a result that looks alarmingly bad. rename the tasks in the model or the activities in the log to make them match. fitness: how much of the recorded behaviour the model can replay, up to 100%. with token replay it combines the tokens the replay had to add and the tokens it left over; with alignments it is the alignment-based fitness. precision: how little behaviour the model allows beyond what happened. a high fitness with a low precision means a permissive model, not a clean process. when precision is skipped, the tile shows "–" and says why. conforming traces: the does not allow or because a required activity was skipped. hover the tile for the same definition. the reference diagram with the result painted onto its tasks. green marks a task the log replays without deviations, and a red scale in five steps marks deviating tasks, darker for more deviations. an amber dashed task is in the model but never in the log, which usually means a name mismatch. with deviation counts on, a badge shows the number of deviations at a task, and "not in log" on such an amber task. with alignments it reads +2 −1: 2 steps happened in the log but are not allowed by the model, and 1 step is required by the model but skipped in the log. a legend under the diagram explains the colours and shows only what is switched on. the diagram has a toolbar in its top right corner with zoom out, zoom in, fit to view, graph settings and fullscreen. a bar chart of the ten activities with the most deviations. it is left out when there are none. two tabs under the explanation of a deviation. by activity: one row per activity with deviations, cases (the cases with at least one deviation there) and a severity bar relative to the worst activity. an activity that occurs in the log links to its activity view, and a model task that never occurs shows the "not in log" badge. with alignments two more columns split the deviations into in log, not in model and in model, skipped in log. token replay does not make that split. by variant: one row per sequence of activities in the log, the most frequent first, with its number of steps, cases, avg fitness with fast. alignments give more precise diagnostics but can take very long on large or varied logs, so mate refuses them above the limits in the configuration. then the run fails with "alignments refused: log has n cases and m variants", and you can switch the technique or raise the limits. on a large log the precision is skipped above the event limit, and fitness and deviations are still computed. raise precision – max events to compute it anyway, at the cost of memory. a token-replay deviation is counted at the model task where the replay had trouble, and an alignment deviation at the activity that was added or skipped, so the two techniques do not give identical counts. only labelled tasks are matched. gateways and events of the model are not coloured. a check says how the log relates to the model, not which of them is right. look at the deviating variants before you change the model or the process. to see how the process actually runs before you check it, use discovery. the module reads the bpmn model, converts it to a petri net with pm4py and replays the log against it. token-based replay follows rozinat and van der aalst (2008): every case is replayed on the net, and missing and remaining tokens measure its deviations. the log fitness combines them as 0.5 times one minus the missing tokens over the consumed tokens, plus 0.5 times one minus the remaining tokens over the produced tokens. alignments, as surveyed by carmona, van dongen and weidlich (2022), instead find the cheapest way to match each case to a run of the model, where a step in the log only or in the model only is a deviation. precision measures how much of the model's behaviour the log actually uses. activity names are unified with the model's spelling before the replay, and the diagram colours come from the per-activity deviation counts. the formal citations are in the info popover next to the module name.

cv4cdd finds out when your process changed. it turns the log into an image of how alike the process was in different periods and lets a trained image model mark the changes. you get a list of drifts with their type, time and confidence, and a map that shows where the model saw them. you suspect that the process was changed, or changed by itself, and you want to know when, and whether it was a single switch, a gradual rollout, a series of small changes or a pattern that comes back. you want the periods before and after a change to compare. use the detected times as the basis for a comparison in process comparison, or look at performance over time, which can shade the detected drift periods behind its trend. you want to know why the process changed. cv4cdd says when and what kind, not why; concept drift explainer takes the detections further. you want recurring calendar patterns, such as busy weeks that look alike, or the trend of one metric. use temporal mapper or performance over time. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 200 events and at least 20 cases. only those three columns are used. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. a detection model has to be installed. mate ships none: an administrator can pin one for everyone under admin → controls, or anyone can upload one on the module's settings page (see settings). without a model the first run fails with "no cv4cdd detection model is available." and the page offers retry. there is no run button. the first time you open the module for a process, and again when the log's data has changed since the last run, mate starts the detection. it shows "computing cv4cdd - concept drift detection…" with a progress bar and a cancel button before the panel appears. models are large, about 0.5 gb each, so a run can take a while. this page has no filter bar. a filter applied on the log's events tab narrows the events the detection reads, and applying or clearing it makes a module you have already opened compute again. everything runs on your mate server, so the module is safe for confidential logs. the panel has no controls. the settings sit on the module's page: open module settings in the sidebar and choose this module. the detection model card stands above the configuration card. upload model adds a pretrained model to the platform. it accepts a .tar.zst archive that contains a tensorflow savedmodel, and the model is shared with every account. the name comes from the file name, and a name that already exists is refused until you delete the old model. if your account has no model selected yet, the one you upload is selected automatically. the list below shows every installed model with its size. choose one to use it with your account. the choice is saved at once, together with any values in the configuration card that you changed but did not save yet. the model in use is marked in use. without a choice, mate picks an installed model itself. the trash icon deletes a model from disk for every account after you confirm. when an administrator pins a model, the card shows admin-controlled: the choice and deletion are read-only, and uploads stay possible. the authors publish models and the training dataset on hugging face. save the values with save configuration. an administrator can lock the card, which makes it read-only. saving does not start a run and does not change detections that already exist: new values apply the next time detection runs, for example after the log's data has changed. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | number of windows | 200 | how many windows the log is cut into (50 to 500). the model was trained at 200, so change it only if your log has very few cases. | | detection confidence threshold | 0.5 | the lowest confidence a detection needs to be reported (0.1 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05). a detection counts when its confidence is above the threshold. lower values report more drifts, including more false alarms. | if no stored detections exist, the page reads "no drifts detected yet". otherwise the panel shows two cards: detected drifts on the left and drift map on the right. the card header repeats the confidence threshold and the number of windows of the run, for example confidence ≥ 50% · 200 windows. below it, one badge per drift type counts the detections, for example "sudden · 2". if nothing passed the threshold, the card reads "the model didn't find any drifts above the confidence threshold." the table lists the detections in chronological order, and for the same start by confidence: type: sudden, gradual, incremental or recurring. hover the label for a short explanation. a sudden drift is a single point where the process abruptly changes. a gradual drift is one where old and new variants co-exist for a while before the switch completes. an incremental drift is a series of small adjustments over time. a recurring drift is an earlier process version that returns and replaces the current one. start and end: the start times of the first case in the first and in the last window of the detection. a sudden drift is a single point, so both are equal. because a window holds many cases, the real change can lie anywhere inside it. confidence: how sure the model is, with one decimal. treat low values as uncertain and check them against the drift map. a picture of how alike the process was in every pair of windows. the windows are equal groups of cases in the order the cases started, and both axes run through them, with the oldest at the top left. a bright pixel means the two windows look alike, a dark one means they differ. the diagonal is always bright, because a window is compared with itself. the scale is relative to the most different pair in this log, so a dark patch can still be a small difference. blocks of bright pixels along the diagonal are stretches of similar behaviour, and a boundary between two blocks is a place where it changed. each detection is a box with a label such as "gradual: 91%". white boxes are sudden drifts, blue gradual, magenta incremental and aqua recurring. if the image is not there yet, the card reads "image not yet available". each card has an info icon with a short explanation and an arrow (open in module) that opens this page. cv drift detections: the number of detections across the run's windows, and one row per detection with its type, its window numbers and its confidence. min confidence (0 to 1, default 0) hides detections below that value on the card only. a card without results asks you to run detection in the module. start with the defaults. raise the confidence threshold if you get too many doubtful drifts, and lower it if you expect one the model misses. both need a new run to take effect. windows hold an equal number of cases, not an equal span of time, so busy periods get many windows and quiet ones few. the last window takes the remainder. with fewer cases than windows, each window gets one case and the remaining windows stay empty, so lower number of windows for small logs. the model was fine-tuned on synthetic logs with known drifts. a detection is a hint to look at that period, not proof of a change. compare the periods in process comparison before you act on it. only the latest run is kept for a log, and it replaces the previous one. detections only mark when behaviour shifted. use concept drift explainer for possible causes. cv4cdd encodes the log as a similarity matrix and treats drift detection as object detection on that image. the cases are put in order of their first event and cut into the chosen number of windows. for each window it counts how often each activity is directly followed by each other activity. it then computes the cosine distance between the counts of every two windows and draws the matrix with the viridis colour scale. a fine-tuned object detector of the retinanet family looks at the image and returns boxes with a drift type and a confidence. boxes above the threshold are mapped back from pixels to windows and then to the start time of the first case in each window. the method is the one of kraus and van der aa (2024), whose cv4cdd models and training data are published on hugging face. the formal citations are in the info popover next to the module name.

discovery mines your event log into process models. it shows how cases actually run as a directly-follows graph (dfg), a petri net, a process tree, a prefix tree, a heuristics net and a bpmn diagram, so you can see the real flow of work, its most frequent paths and its rare detours. you want to see how the process really runs: which activities occur, in which order and how often. the dfg is the place to start. you need a formal model, such as a petri net, a process tree or a bpmn file, for example as a reference model for conformance checking. you want timing. discovery only shows the mean time between two activities on the dfg; for cycle times and bottlenecks use performance, and to compare two groups of cases use process comparison. your events refer to several object types at once (orders, items, invoices). on an object-centric log discovery's card is greyed out as unavailable; use object-centric discovery. the log must be case-centric, with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 50 events and at least 2 cases. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. nothing else is needed: no model to upload, no api key and no external service. every model is mined from your events inside mate. mate computes discovery in the background right after you import a log (an administrator can change this), so it is usually ready when you open it. if it is not, you see "computing discovery…" with a progress bar and a cancel button. the run happens once; next time it is instant. a failed or cancelled run is reported on the page with a retry or run button. everything else is mined when you first choose it: the ilp miner, im infrequent at a noise threshold other than 0.2, the heuristics net at thresholds other than its defaults, the bpmn frequency filter above 0, and the backbone and layered dfg layouts. the ilp miner is refused on logs with more than 30 distinct activities or more than 5,000 cases. every view is a canvas with a toolbar in its top right corner: zoom out, zoom in, fit to view, graph settings (the sliders icon), reset layout and fullscreen. the tables below list what graph settings holds for each view. the prefix tree has no settings. a mini-map appears at the bottom right while you pan or zoom. cards you drag stay where you drop them until you press reset layout and confirm. on the dfg that clears the moved cards of every discovery view for the log; on the other views only that view's. the bpmn diagram cannot be dragged, and its reset button is called reset view. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | activities | auto | a slider that keeps the most frequent activities, from the single most frequent (left) to all (right). its read-out shows visible / total, for example 8 / 16. auto keeps activities up to the knee of the cumulative frequency curve and never fewer than 5 (or all, when there are fewer). dragging the slider turns auto off; spot backlogs, seasonality and changes in behaviour. you want to know whether work is piling up: arrivals that stay above completions mean the number of open cases is growing. you want to spot seasonality, batch processing or a shift in which activities dominate when, or to check whether a process redesign changed how work arrives and gets done. you want durations rather than volumes. use performance over time for cycle time and throughput per period. for periods whose activity patterns look alike, use temporal mapper, and to detect drift explicitly, use cv4cdd. the module needs a case-centric event log with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 50 events and at least 2 cases. only those three columns are read; the optional end_timestamp column is not used, and events whose timestamp cannot be read are ignored. the first time you open the module for a process, mate computes the default series (auto granularity). it shows "computing log evolution…" with a progress bar and a cancel button before the panel appears, and afterwards the page opens at once. other granularities and the dotted chart are computed when they are first shown. three controls sit in the bar above the charts. each loads or redraws only the charts it belongs to. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | granularity | auto | the calendar period each point stands how many of the most frequent activities get their own band in activity mix over time; the rest are summed into one band called other. only that chart changes, and nothing is loaded again. | | dotted-chart points | 8,000 | 2,000, 4,000, 8,000, 12,000 or 20,000. the most events the dotted chart draws. when the log has more events, a sample of that size is drawn. only the dotted chart is whose first event falls in the period, and completions counts the cases whose last event falls in it. every case appears once in each line, so each line adds up to the number of cases. where arrivals drops below zero and always ends at zero, because every case has a last event. a stacked area chart of the number of events per activity in each period. these are event counts, not shares: the height of the whole stack is the number of events in the period. the most frequent activities of the whole log get their own band, up to activities shown, and all other activities are summed into a grey band called other, which appears only when the log has more activities than bands. the legend names the bands, and hovering shows each band's count. a band that grows or vanishes marks a change in how the process is run, and sometimes a change in how events are recorded. an empty chart reads "no activity mix for this log yet." the classic dotted chart: one dot per event. the horizontal position is the time of the event, and the vertical position is the case, ordered by the time of its first event, with the earliest case at the top. the vertical axis shows each case's rank, starting at 0, not its case id. the colour is the activity: the 12 most frequent activities of the log keep their own colour and all others share a grey called other. all events of one case sit in one row, so a steady flow you want to know what differs, not only whether something does. pcomp returns one p-value and no picture. for the overlaid process map, the variant differences and the per-activity changes, use process comparison. you want to compare speed. pcomp does not register waiting or processing times in mate, so compare the performance figures of both logs instead. in this version both tests compare activity sequences only. the permutation test is the timed variant, but mate does not hand it start timestamps, so every event counts as instantaneous. two logs with the same traces and very different timing show no difference. the log you open the module on is the baseline. it must be case-centric, with case_id, activity and timestamp columns, at least 50 events and at least 2 cases. otherwise the module's card in the process's module list shows an unavailable badge and cannot be opened; hover the card to read the reason. you need a second log in your account that is ready and case-centric. object-centric logs and the baseline itself are not offered. if there is none, the panel says "no other ready case-centric logs available. import a second log first." nothing is precomputed. a test runs only when you start it, as a background job with a progress bar. this page has no filter bar. each log is used as it stands. a filter applied on a log's events tab narrows that log in the entry shows the log's name and its number of cases. the two test tabs appear once you have picked one. | start it with run permutation test. | setting | default | what it changes | | --- | --- | --- | | distribution size | 1000 | how many random permutations make up the reference distribution. the field is set up for 100 to 20000 in steps of 100; typed values are not checked. more permutations give
